newsitem.title: USA: Clinton sidesteps question of giving Lebanon arms.
newsitem.headline: Clinton sidesteps question of giving Lebanon arms.

text.p: Taking a brief rest from his re-election campaign, President Bill Clinton met Lebanese Prime Minster Rafik al-Hariri on Friday but sidestepped the question of giving Lebanon the military hardware it seeks.

Clinton told reporters before the White House meeting that he would discuss Lebanon's request for military equipment -- including helicopters, armoured personel carriers, aircraft and communications gear -- and make the appropriate decision.
Asked after the meeting what Clinton had said about the request, Hariri told reporters: "I didn't get any answer about that."
A White House official told reporters afterward that the two men had not discussed "specific weapons systems."
"There was a general discussion of the security situation and the prime minister articulated very forcefully the need that he sees to have an effective security force," he said.
"There wasn't a discussion (of) specific weapons systems or specific transfers that might be required for that to take place," he added.
Hariri also came to Washington with a second request, that the ban on U.S. citizens travelling to Lebanon be lifted, but did not get a definitive answer on this.

The White House official said the United States wanted to be in a position to lift the ban but could only do so if it was convinced that the threat of abductions of U.S. citizens had receded sufficiently.
He said the ban was reviewed every six months, adding that the next such deliberation would take place in February.
The United States, which saw a series of U.S. citizens kidnapped in Lebanon during the 1980s, imposed the ban to protect Americans from such abductions.
The U.S. official also stressed the United States' long-standing position that it is committed to Lebanon's territorial integrity.

Syria has 35,000 troops stationed in Lebanon, while Israel has about 1,000 soldiers in the southern part of the country, where it maintains a buffer zone along with about 3,000 troops from its ally, the South Lebanon Army militia.
